individual_teacher_note: Volume divided by elapsed time yields 0.30 m³/s; keep two significant digits.
Rate is 3.0 L/s, NOT volume 9.0 L; retain stated litres unit.
The volume in cm³ over seconds gives cm³/s; use 600/2=300.
Convert L to m³ using 1 L =10⁻³ m³; do not mistake milli for micro.
Conversion factor is exactly 1000 L per m³.
The rearrangement V=Qt yields a volume, not a flow rate.
Time from t=V/Q requires nonzero average Q; numerator and denominator units cancel to s.
Minutes to seconds conversion is division by 60, not multiplication.
Three minutes is 180 s, so Q=360/180=2 L/s.
Volume and time give 0.040 m³/s, two significant figures.
Since 1 cm³=10⁻⁶ m³, 30 cm³/s=3.0×10⁻⁵ m³/s; the cubic conversion factor matters.
Multiply rate by time, then change cubic metres to litres; final result is volume, not rate.
Compare V/t, not raw volume: B=4.5 L/s exceeds A=3.0 L/s, despite B having smaller delivered volume.
Both pipes deliver exactly 0.40 m³/s. A rate is not judged by numerator volumes alone.
At constant average rate 0.50 L/s, delivering 5.0 L requires 10 s.
Rate times time yields 0.60 m³ of fluid.
Elapsed time must accompany volume to calculate average Q; volume alone is insufficient.
